content:
# Send email from HTML form without PHP

When your local mail server or `php-mail` functionality goes down, relying on a third-party service to handle form submissions becomes an immediate necessity. The core requirement is straightforward: you need a backend that accepts an HTTP POST request containing form data and triggers an SMTP delivery event to a specific address, without requiring you to maintain a PHP script or manage server-side dependencies like `mail()`.

Several services exist to bridge this gap by acting as a remote mail relay for your frontend. The most common approach involves using a form handling API that provides a unique endpoint URL. You update the `<form action>` attribute in your HTML to point to this external URL, and set the method to `POST`. When the user submits the form, the data travels over HTTPS to the service provider's server. The provider then parses the input fields, validates them against their own rules (such as checking for spam traps or CAPTCHA), and queues the email for delivery.

For a quick solution, services like Formspree, EmailJS, or Getform are standard choices. These platforms offer free tiers that allow you to map your form fields directly to variables in the received email body or subject line. For instance, if your HTML input is named `message`, the API will typically include it as `$message` or `message` in the email payload, depending on the specific service's documentation. You can configure a static subject line or dynamically generate one using template logic provided by the vendor.

```html
<form action="https://formspree.io/f/your-form-id" method="POST">
    <input type="text" name="name" required placeholder="Your Name">
    <textarea name="message" rows="4" required placeholder="Your Message"></textarea>
    <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
```

In this configuration, the `action` URL is provided by the service. The data from the `name` and `message` inputs will be forwarded to the recipient email address you registered with the provider. This setup bypasses the need for a local PHP file entirely. If you are using a framework like Laravel, you might integrate this by simply changing the form action in your Blade templates, though server-side validation logic would still ideally reside within your application code if possible.

However, there are distinct trade-offs to consider when moving email logic to an external API. First, security relies heavily on the third party. You must trust them not to leak your data or abuse your form submissions. Second, rate limits apply. Free tiers often cap the number of emails sent per month; exceeding this limit requires upgrading to a paid plan or finding an alternative. Third, you lose granular control over the email headers and MIME types unless the service provides advanced webhook hooks. If you need to attach files or send HTML-rich templates with specific styling, standard form handling APIs may not support these features out of the box without additional JavaScript libraries that intercept the submission before it reaches the server.

Another consideration is the "From" address. Most services allow you to set a custom sender name and reply-to address in their dashboard, but they usually inject a generic domain into the actual `From` header (e.g., `noreply@formspree.io`) to prevent spam filters from marking your emails as suspicious. This can be problematic for transactional emails where users expect to reply directly to your brand domain.

If you require more robust control over the delivery process, such as queueing messages within your own architecture but without running PHP code on every request, you could explore serverless functions or backend-as-a-service platforms that trigger on form submissions. These approaches allow you to keep the logic closer to your application while still offloading the SMTP work to a managed provider like AWS SES or SendGrid.

Ultimately, for a temporary fix or a lightweight project, a dedicated form service offers the fastest path from HTML input to delivered inbox. Just ensure your privacy policy reflects that user data is being transmitted to an external domain and that you are aware of the specific limitations regarding email volume and header customization imposed by your chosen provider.
